name: Absalom
bio:
Absalom was David's third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3) — a strikingly handsome prince whose festering resentment over his sister's violation would eventually erupt into open rebellion against his own father.

## 📖 Core Story: Revenge, Exile, and an Uneasy Return

When Absalom's full sister Tamar was raped by their half-brother Amnon, Absalom said nothing to Amnon at all, "neither good nor bad," while hatred quietly built in him for two full years (2 Samuel 13:1-22). At a sheep-shearing feast he hosted at Baal-hazor, Absalom invited all the king's sons, then had his servants strike down Amnon once he was merry with wine — carrying out his planned revenge in front of his brothers, who fled in terror, briefly leaving David to fear all his sons were dead (2 Samuel 13:23-33). Absalom himself fled to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and stayed there three years while David mourned and his longing to see Absalom slowly grew (2 Samuel 13:34-39).

Noticing the king's heart turning toward Absalom, Joab arranged for a wise woman of Tekoa to tell David a crafted parable about a surviving son threatened with death, maneuvering David into declaring that the banished should be brought home — and, once he saw through the scheme, into approving Absalom's return (2 Samuel 14:1-21). Joab brought Absalom back to Jerusalem, but David refused to see his face for two more years; renowned throughout Israel for his flawless beauty and famously heavy hair, Absalom grew three sons and a daughter he named Tamar after his wronged sister. Frustrated at being shut out, Absalom had Joab's field set on fire to force an audience, which finally won him reconciliation and a kiss from the king (2 Samuel 14:23-33).

Rather than settle, Absalom began positioning himself for the throne: he kept chariots, horses, and fifty runners, rose early to intercept petitioners at the city gate, told each that their case was just but that the king had appointed no one to hear them, and declared he wished he were judge so he could give everyone justice — "so Absalom stole the hearts of the people of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:1-6). After four years of this, he asked David's permission to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow, then used it to launch open rebellion, sending secret messengers throughout Israel to proclaim him king and drawing David's own counselor Ahithophel into the conspiracy (2 Samuel 15:7-12). David, forced to flee Jerusalem, left the city to Absalom, who entered it in triumph as David's exile and the long, painful struggle to reclaim his throne begin — a story told in detail through the rest of 2 Samuel.
